axes-points-s1.title: Calle Verde Taco Truck: price and tacos sold

table.caption: Tacos sold per day at each price (invented data for practice)

items.q: On a market graph in this course, which variable goes on the horizontal axis?
options: The price of the good
The number of sellers
The quantity of the good
The time of year

why.correct: Market graphs put quantity across the bottom and price up the side. Mixing them up flips every curve.
options: Price goes on the vertical axis of a market graph.
The number of sellers is not an axis of a market graph.
Right: quantity runs along the horizontal axis.
Time is not one of the two axes on a market graph.

items.q: A graph has tacos sold per day on the horizontal axis and price per taco on the vertical axis. What does the ordered pair (60, 4) describe?
options: 60 tacos sold at a price of \$4
4 tacos sold at a price of \$60
A price of \$60 for 4 days
64 tacos sold in total

why.correct: The first number is the horizontal value (tacos sold) and the second is the vertical value (price).
options: Right: horizontal value first, then vertical.
This reverses the order: the first number is the horizontal value.
Neither axis measures days.
An ordered pair is two separate values, never a sum.

items.q: With tacos sold on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis, which ordered pair plots the row for a price of \$2?

why.correct: At \$2 the truck sells 100 tacos. Tacos sold is the horizontal value, so it comes first: (100, 2).
options: This puts the price first, but price is on the vertical axis.
The price is \$2, not \$200.
At \$2 the truck sells 100 tacos, not 2.
Right: (tacos sold, price) = (100, 2).

items.q: What relationship between price and tacos sold does the table show?
options: A direct relationship: as the price rises, more tacos are sold
An inverse relationship: as the price rises, fewer tacos are sold
No relationship: tacos sold stay the same
A direct relationship, because both columns hold numbers

why.correct: As the price goes from \$1 to \$5, tacos sold fall from 120 to 40. One rises while the other falls: inverse.
options: Tacos sold fall as the price rises, so the relationship is not direct.
Right: price up, tacos sold down.
Tacos sold change in every row.
A relationship is about how the values move together, not about both being numbers.

items.q: How many more tacos a day does the truck sell at a price of \$2 than at a price of \$4?

why.correct: Read both rows: 100 tacos at \$2 and 60 at \$4. The difference is $100 - 60 = 40$ tacos.

mistakes.why: That adds the two rows. The question asks how many MORE, so subtract the smaller from the larger.

items.q: Which of these points lie on the graph of the table, with tacos sold across and price up? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Each row gives (tacos sold, price): (120, 1), (100, 2), (80, 3), (60, 4) and (40, 5).
options: Right: 120 tacos at \$1.
Right: 80 tacos at \$3.
This reverses the order; the horizontal value (tacos) comes first.
At \$1 the truck sells 120 tacos, not 40; 40 tacos go with \$5.

items.q: Label both axes and both curves of this market graph.

why.correct: On a market graph, price goes on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. The downward curve is D and the upward curve is S.

items.q: Place point X at a larger quantity and a higher price than the point where the two curves meet.

why.correct: A larger quantity is farther right on the horizontal axis; a higher price is farther up the vertical axis. So X goes up and to the right of the meeting point.

items.q: A part-time worker earns more the more hours she works. If hours go on the horizontal axis and weekly pay on the vertical axis, how do the points look?
options: They fall to the right: an inverse relationship
They rise to the right: a direct relationship
They form a flat line: no relationship
They rise to the left: an inverse relationship

why.correct: More hours bring more pay, so both values grow together and the points rise to the right.
options: Falling points would mean more hours bring less pay.
Right: both rise together.
A flat line would mean pay stays the same whatever the hours.
Points that rise to the left fall to the right, which is inverse; here both rise together.

items.q: A student graphs the taco table with price on the horizontal axis and tacos sold on the vertical axis. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: either axis may hold either variable on a market graph
The relationship will change from inverse to direct
The five rows will no longer plot as points
The axes are reversed from the market-graph convention, so the curve will not match the graphs in the course

why.correct: The numbers still plot, and the relationship is still inverse, but market graphs always put quantity across and price up. Reversed axes give a graph a reader cannot score.
options: Market graphs follow one convention so readers can check them.
Swapping axes does not turn an inverse relationship into a direct one: the points still fall as you move right.
All five rows still plot as points; they are just on the wrong axes.
Right: the convention is quantity across, price up.

items.q: A point sits at (0, 7) on a graph with quantity across and price up. Where is it?
options: On the vertical axis, at a price of 7
On the horizontal axis, at a quantity of 7
At the origin, where the axes meet
Off the graph, because 0 is not a value

why.correct: A horizontal value of 0 means no distance to the right, so the point sits on the vertical axis, 7 units up.
options: Right: zero across, 7 up.
A point on the horizontal axis has a vertical value of 0, like (7, 0).
The origin is (0, 0).
Zero is a value; it places the point on an axis.

items.q: Point M is (30, 8) and point N is (50, 6) on a graph with quantity across and price up. Which statement is correct?
options: N shows a smaller quantity and a higher price than M
M and N show the same quantity
N shows a larger quantity and a lower price than M
M shows a larger quantity because its second number is bigger

why.correct: Compare first numbers for quantity (50 is more than 30) and second numbers for price (6 is less than 8).
options: This reads the pairs backward.
The first numbers, 30 and 50, differ.
Right: 50 > 30 and 6 < 8.
The second number is the price, not the quantity.
